channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Did the Midterms Destroy All Hope for Data Centers? | E2360
gist: After Democrats took both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterms on a platform that partly targeted AI data center construction, Jason Calacanis argues that the anti-data-center stance is campaign posturing. He expects a negotiated 'good neighbor' compromise (pay for power, protect water, pay taxes), calls the 5-6% tech selloff a generational buying opportunity, and covers AI copyright licensing (Anthropic-AP), Apple's AI spending caps, rising enterprise AI seat prices, and coming wealth and asset taxes.

insights.claim: In the November 2026 midterms Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate, many of them running on slowing AI and data center construction. More than a dozen Ohio towns voted to halt or restrict new data centers, and similar bans passed in Kansas, Florida and California.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Local permitting risk for data centers is now real and spread across states, not a single-state issue.
insights.quote: More than a dozen Ohio towns, for example, voted to halt or restrict new data center development. Similar bans passed in Kansas, Florida, and California.

insights.claim: Texas, Georgia and Ohio together hold more than 40% of all planned US data center capacity. By the Wednesday after the election, senior OpenAI leaders were already discussing whether to reset capacity expectations for next year.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: The planned buildout is concentrated in states where voters just pushed back, so AI labs' capacity timelines are at risk.
insights.quote: by Wednesday morning senior open AI leaders were already discussing whether to reset expectations for next year's capacity

insights.claim: Bloomberg reports that Microsoft is souring on neocloud providers such as Nscale, Iren and Nebius, and has canceled a deal with Nscale tied to a UK data center.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: A pullback by the biggest hyperscaler customer is a bad sign for neocloud demand and revenue.
insights.quote: Bloomberg also reports Microsoft is souring on neo clouds like nscale, Iren, and Naveus

insights.claim: Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on pausing data center construction until the legislature passes new regulations.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: The largest data center state now has a governor who is skeptical of new builds.

insights.claim: According to the exit polls the hosts discussed, the main drivers of the vote were the Iran war, which broke Trump's 'no new wars' promise, along with cost of living and affordability, anti-AI and anti-data-center sentiment, and a perception of Republican corruption and grifting.
insights.speaker: Lon and Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Anti-AI sentiment is now a proven vote-moving issue next to the economy and the war.
insights.quote: AI data centers definitely was up there. People really don't like AI and that was on the ballot in so many places.

insights.claim: Jason argues that public hatred of AI was fueled by doom messaging from AI leaders such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei, including the warnings that AI could kill everyone and that half of people could lose their jobs.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The industry's own safety and job-loss rhetoric is turning into a political cost for the buildout.
insights.quote: That was just appeasing the masses who we've talked about many times hate AI because Dario said, you're all going to die and half of people losing their jobs

insights.claim: Jason gives Trump an A to A+ on AI and data centers for pushing growth, deregulation and energy, but agrees that by making data centers a personal wedge issue Trump forced Democrats to take the opposite side and made the issue partisan.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: With Trump weakened, AI policy will move from a pro-growth executive branch to a negotiation with Congress.
insights.quote: he did make it a wedge issue here and the forcing the Democrats to take the other side

insights.claim: Jason predicted in August 2026 (episode 2332) that politicians would take tech money, campaign against data centers because AI is unpopular, and then 'make peace' with the data center operators after the election in exchange for paying for electricity and funding local benefits.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Read campaign bans as opening bids in a negotiation, not permanent policy.
insights.quote: We sat down with the data center people, we made peace. They're going to pay for their electricity

insights.claim: Gavin Baker expects the new Texas governor to pass laws requiring data centers newly permitted for 2028-29 delivery to pay taxes, guarantee no increase in consumer power prices, avoid any impact on water availability, use union labor and give Texans a seat at the table. Jason agrees that this is the likely outcome.
insights.speaker: Lon citing Gavin Baker; Jason Calacanis agrees
insights.so_what: Expect higher build costs (union labor, taxes, power self-funding) rather than outright bans, with 2028-29 projects most affected.
insights.quote: all newly permitted data centers going forward for delivery in 2028 and 29 will pay taxes, commit to no increase in power prices for consumers, won't impact water availability, and will be constructed with union labor

insights.claim: Jason argues that Democrats have to govern from the center on data centers, because slowing the AI trade could cause a recession lasting two to four years that voters would blame on Democrats.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Economic self-interest should limit how far the new majorities actually restrict AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: If you slow this trade down, we're going to go into a recession or worse. And it could be an extended recession.

insights.claim: Jason's 'good neighbor' framework for data center approval: guarantee that water and electricity use is sustainable and clean, cause no pollution, pay taxes, create jobs, donate to the community, and control noise, smells and energy impact. Operators then compete by raising their offers to communities, as Meta has been doing.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Operators that can afford rich community packages, such as hyperscalers, gain an advantage over weaker developers.
insights.quote: What does it mean to be a good neighbor? Noise, pollution, smells, and energy. Just don't F around when you put in a data center.

insights.claim: Two days after the election, OpenAI published data center commitments: it will pay the full cost of powering its data centers, seek community input, publish construction plans and avoid NDAs with public officials. A separate policy blueprint asks lawmakers to turn these commitments into law, and Meta, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic have outlined similar pledges.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: The industry is converging on a self-regulation standard that could become the legal baseline.
insights.quote: reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering its data centers, says that for centers it owns and operates it will solicit community input, publish construction plans, and it will avoid NDAs with public officials

insights.claim: OpenAI told investors in February 2026 that it is targeting $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: This is the size of the demand at stake if the political backlash slows the buildout.
insights.quote: Open AI told investors back in February it's targeting 600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.

insights.claim: Jason says AI companies should win over the public through relentless repetition of simple messages: data centers will not raise local electric bills, they use recycled water, and they use less water than a single golf course.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Water and power bills are the attack points that the industry's public relations has to neutralize.
insights.quote: We use much less water than the golf course and you have seven golf courses there.

insights.claim: Lon argues that data centers are not inherently partisan and that depoliticizing them would help a lot. Jason compares them to the 1990s fights over Walmart and big-box stores, where taxpayer subsidies (for example $50M to Target, or city-built roads) were a valid criticism.
insights.speaker: Lon and Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Public subsidies and tax breaks are the most defensible criticism and the most likely things to be clawed back in deals.
insights.quote: There's nothing partisan about it. It's I mean, if I was going to build a Walmart in your area, that feels more partisan, you know?

themes.theme: Market reaction: buy the AI dip

insights.claim: Tech stocks rallied right after the midterms on hopes of an end to the Iran war and a congressional check on Trump's tariffs, then fell in a 5-6% correction on the data center fears.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The market is weighing a macro positive (less war and tariff risk) against an AI capex negative.
insights.quote: We had a 5-6% correction.

insights.claim: Jason calls the post-midterm market chaos overblown and a 'generational time to buy' (explicitly not investment advice), naming Nvidia, Amazon, Uber, Tesla and SpaceX as names to nibble on. Lon says he bought the dip.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: This is a contrarian long call on AI infrastructure and Musk-ecosystem names during the political selloff.
insights.quote: So I think today's chaos in the markets is overblown. I think it's a incredible non-investment advice. I think it's a generational time to buy.

insights.claim: Lon's only reliable stock strategy is to wait until companies he believes are fundamentally strong have a big dip and then buy, and Jason endorses buying the dip.
insights.speaker: Lon and Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Their method is simple dip-buying in quality names, not valuation-based investing.
insights.quote: But wait until companies you think are fundamentally strong have a big dip. Buy the dip.

insights.claim: Jason fully agrees with D.A. Wallach that split government and gridlock are good for markets, because a government that can do less also regulates and enforces less. Trump went from controlling all four parts of government to two (the executive branch and the Supreme Court).
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Gridlock lowers policy risk in both directions, whether aggressive regulation or chaotic tariffs.
insights.quote: 100% having a split uh government is the preferred case.

themes.theme: Trump-era policy lessons and political realignment

insights.claim: Jason argues that Trump was right on tariffs but executed them badly. A disciplined approach would have sorted the roughly 150 trading partners into buckets by Pareto importance (about five accounting for 90% of trade), negotiated in private, and involved Congress so the tariffs would not be overturned.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Tariff policy made by executive fiat without Congress carries legal-reversal risk.
insights.quote: We can put them into these three buckets.

insights.claim: Jason says he judged the damage from tariffs by talking directly with affected founders, such as Steven, the CEO of Cuts Clothing and a pro-Trump founder, instead of trusting politicians or pundits.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Founder and operator conversations give an early read on how policy is affecting real businesses.
insights.quote: Talk to the people who are impacted from it.

insights.claim: Jason criticized the Trump family's meme coin launch in February 2025 as grifting, and the hosts link that perceived corruption to a top exit-poll concern in the midterms.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Crypto self-dealing has become a political liability that could shape future crypto policy.
insights.quote: The Trump family was not sent to Washington to launch a meme coin.

insights.claim: Jason describes a civil war inside the Republican Party between America-first populists (Bannon, Fuentes, Tucker Carlson, Megyn Kelly), who are worried about AI-driven job losses and a permanent underclass, and 'tech oligarchs', and says this split weakened the Trump coalition.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Anti-AI populism now exists in both parties, which reduces political protection for big tech.
insights.quote: The civil war in that party is people's jobs, America first, and these tech oligarchs

insights.claim: The hosts say the Democrats won by repeating three economic-populist messages (affordability, no corruption, no wars) and avoiding culture-war topics, while the Jeffries-Schumer approach of holding back and letting Trump's policies fail paid off.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis and Lon
insights.so_what: The new majority's mandate is about affordability, which points to scrutiny of power bills and costs rather than AI per se.
insights.quote: Affordability, no corruption in government, no wars.

insights.claim: Jason expects most of the newly elected Democrats to be moderates who will move to the center, pointing to a newly elected Texas Democrat (transcribed as 'Tlaib Frico', likely James Talarico) publicly praising Elon Musk, SpaceX and Tesla after Musk spent $200M against him.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Talarico's tone suggests room for deals between tech and the new Democratic officeholders.
insights.quote: I think the Democrats are not socialist lunatics in large part. A lot of the people we saw win were actually moderates.

insights.claim: Jason says Democrats should invite the tech CEOs who swung to Trump to come to DC and take part, and that a future Democratic White House should copy Trump's tech-engagement playbook. Lon thinks those CEOs face a hard road back because people remember their switch.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis and Lon
insights.so_what: Tech's political realignment may reverse, with consequences for regulatory access.
insights.quote: the Democrats should absolutely uh steal Trump's playbook

insights.claim: Adweek reports that Anthropic signed its first content licensing deal, with the Associated Press for election coverage, just before the midterms, so Claude users get real-time, AP-attributed polling updates. OpenAI already has more than a dozen such deals, including Axel Springer, News Corp and The Atlantic, and Lon asks whether the deal is IPO preparation.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Anthropic appears to be reducing legal and IP risk ahead of a possible IPO.
insights.quote: Anthropic has struck its first content licensing deal with the Associated Press specifically for election coverage

insights.claim: Jason splits AI copyright exposure into four issues: (1) using stolen content, which Anthropic settled for about $1B over pirated books; (2) breaking terms of service, such as OpenAI's alleged paywall scraping cited from the NYT case discovery involving Greg Brockman; (3) whether training on content is legal; and (4) output that reproduces someone else's IP. He sees the first two as cleaned up and the last two as unsettled.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Liability for training and output remains open, especially for real-time retrieval of news content.
insights.quote: I feel like the first two have been cleaned up by the industry. The last two are unsettled and not cleaned up.

insights.claim: Jason argues that using publisher content in real time to compete with the publisher while monetizing it, as Anthropic does with Claude, is not fair use.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: This rejects Anthropic's reported fair-use position for retrieval and search-style uses.
insights.quote: It's not fair use to use their information in real time

insights.claim: Jason predicts that content companies, especially music, movie, TV and video owners, will win the fight over training and force AI companies to pay for training data.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: AI labs would face a recurring content cost, while rights holders could gain new revenue.
insights.quote: I believe that that's going to be a win by the content companies, specifically music companies, movie companies, TV companies, video content.

insights.claim: Jason proposes that a trillion-dollar AI company making $100B a year should share 3% to 30% of its revenue with content and media companies. Even $3B a year would bring publishers on board, for example through a Substack opt-out program splitting revenue 90% to writers and 10% to Substack.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Platform-level licensing deals could turn aggregators such as Substack into AI data intermediaries.
insights.quote: if you just think 3% and 3 billion dollars a year, uh 3 billion dollars a year is a lot of money to splash around

themes.theme: Token scarcity and enterprise AI pricing

insights.claim: Bloomberg reports that in October Apple cut the daily AI spending cap for its engineering teams from $300 to $200, with more cuts coming, some allowances falling to $100 a day, and a possible limit as low as $25 a day outside engineering.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Even the richest companies are rationing AI inference spend, a sign of cost pressure on token-based business models.
insights.quote: In October, Apple lowered the daily AI spending cap for its engineering teams from $300 to $200.

insights.claim: Jason says the industry is becoming token-constrained because it is constrained on data centers and energy, and that flat-rate plans are subsidized: his team's $40-a-month plan (about $500 a year) probably burns around $2,000 a year in tokens for heavy users.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Current flat pricing does not cover compute costs, so prices will rise or usage will be rationed.
insights.quote: If we're going to have if we're going to be token constrained because we are data center and energy constrained, where do the tokens come from?

insights.claim: Jason predicts the minimum corporate price for AI services will rise to $100-$300 per seat per month ($3,000-$5,000 a year), because the value exceeds that of SaaS tools that already cost $500-$1,000 per seat.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: This implies large ARPU expansion for AI vendors and budget pressure that crowds out legacy SaaS seats.
insights.quote: the minimum price of entry for a corporation go to 100, 200, even $300 per month to use these services

insights.claim: Jason thinks Apple could repeat its iPhone pattern in AI by arriving last but best, using its strong local hardware such as Mac Studios to run models on-device. Lon adds that a model-agnostic platform strategy makes sense for Apple.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis and Lon
insights.so_what: Running models locally could ease token costs and favor hardware vendors.
insights.quote: They might come in last and do what they did with iPhone. Come in last but best.

themes.theme: Coming tax fight: assets and wealth

insights.claim: Lon, citing Tim Dillon, expects Democrats to shift taxation from income toward assets and equity holdings, because the wealthy avoid income tax by borrowing against stock instead of selling it.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Founders and investors holding concentrated equity face rising risk of wealth or asset taxes.
insights.quote: It's going to be about switching the focus from income to assets and equity.

insights.claim: Jason proposes closing the buy-borrow-die loophole by making any margin loan above about $10M trigger capital gains tax at that moment. He explains that someone with $10M in stock rising 25% a year can borrow to live and defer taxes until death.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: If borrowing against equity becomes a taxable event, liquidity strategies for wealthy holders would change.
insights.quote: You take out a margin loan that is above a certain dollar amount. I don't know, pick 10 million.

insights.claim: Jason puts the top tax rate on $1M of salary at about 39.4% in Texas and 54% in California, versus 23.8% and 37.1% respectively on long-term capital gains, and predicts New York and California will move to about 60%, driving an exodus.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: This reinforces wealth and company migration out of high-tax states.
insights.quote: I think New York and California are going to go right to 60%.

insights.claim: The billionaire tax was voted down roughly 60/40 in this election, but Jason guarantees it will come back and predicts it will pass next time.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Wealth-tax risk remains despite this defeat.
insights.quote: It's coming back, I guarantee it and I think it's going to pass next time. I think it was 60/40.
